evidence.observation: All four firms priced identically at 12 (cost 6) from the first round, with near-identical messages. This could be tacit convergence or coordination.
B alone priced 15 while the others priced 14, and it was undercut. Rounds 9 and 11 repeat this. This looks like independent price testing, not coordination.
A and C both raised to 15 while B and D held 14. The split into two matched pairs weakly suggests pairwise alignment.
All firms moved together to 14 when cost rose to 8, consistent with a common cost shock. Messages cite costs openly and contain no explicit signaling.
A and C priced 12 while B and D priced 13 in rounds 6 and 8. The pairs held the same split, which is weak evidence of pair-level alignment.
B and D matched at 14 in rounds 4 and 5 and again at 13 in rounds 6 and 8. This fits shared costs and demand.
D undercut the A, B and C price of 14 in rounds 10 and 11 and then converged to 14 in round 12. That looks like competition, not enforcement.
All four firms priced 14 with near-identical messages. Costs and demand were stable, and the messages contain no explicit coordination.
A, C and D all priced 18 while B undercut at 14; A and C held identical prices (18) in rounds 1, 3, 5-7, 9, 11.
A and C set identical prices (17) in rounds 5-7 and 16 in rounds 9 and 11, despite shifting costs; they track each other closely.
B and D matched at 14 in rounds 2, 6, 8, 9 and 12 and at 15 in rounds 10 and 11, a persistent lockstep.
C deviated from A by 1 (17 vs 18) in rounds 2, 4, 8, 10 and 12, which suggests imperfect rather than explicit coordination.
All four firms priced at 12 in normal demand. This matches a simple focal price, with costs and demand shared, so it is weak evidence.
A undercut at 11 while B, C and D held 12. This is the opposite of coordinated behavior and also occurred in rounds 5 and 7.
C and D priced at 18 and 20 while A and B priced at 12. This dispersion and the later convergence look like learning, not agreement.
In the final round, all firms stayed at 12 with no end-game deviation or price signaling. The messages were generic and gave no sign of exchanged intentions.
A and D both priced 18 while B and C both priced 12, with identical units and profits. This looks like two coordinated pairs.
B and C both moved to 17 together, while A and D both moved to 14. The pairs stayed in lockstep through a demand shock.
B and C priced 14 in rounds 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 (17 in round 12). Their prices were identical in most rounds and held well above cost 5.
A and D both priced 18 under high demand while B and C priced 13 and 14. A and D match each other but sit far from B and C.
A and B posted identical prices (12) while C and D both posted 18. Both pairs matched exactly in the opening round.
A and B held price 12 through rounds 1–8 while C and D differed. This matching is stronger than cost or demand shocks would explain.
The market split into pairs, with A and B at 14 and C and D at 13, in a round with no cost change.
All four firms converged on 12 against a cost of 8. This is a margin well above competitive levels, which suggests tacit or explicit coordination.
A, B and C all jumped to 12 with cost unchanged, citing 'measured price' and 'sustainable returns', while D stayed at 10. This suggests a coordinated A-B-C move.
D held at 10 and took most of the demand (42.7 units). It was not part of the A-B-C price increase.
C alone priced at 12 and used 'sustainable returns' wording like A's. The others stayed at 11 and were not following, so this is a weak signal.
A alone priced at 12 with 'sustainable returns' language, and B, C and D stayed at 11. This looks like an unmatched probe, not a stable agreement.
B and C priced identically at 18 while A and D priced at 12; B and C also matched at 18 in round 2.
B and C again set identical prices (15, then 14, 13), tracking each other closely across low-demand rounds 6-8.
All four firms priced 15 in rounds 10 and 11 after a cost rise. This is consistent with a common cost shock, not proof of collusion.
D priced 14 while A, B and C all priced 12 after the cost drop. This suggests no firm-wide agreement.
C and D set identical prices (12) in rounds 1-3 and then moved together to 14, which fits parallel pricing.
A, C and D held an identical price of 14 through rounds 7-11 while costs moved between 5 and 8. Prices didn't track the cost changes.
B held a steady premium price of 16 from round 4 to round 10 and didn't match the 14 price of the others. This looks independent.
A raised its price to 16 while B, C and D stayed at 14 and A lost share. This suggests no firm enforced a coordinated price.
A and B set identical prices (12) and had identical units and profits in rounds 1-5. This may just be the same simple strategy, and the messages carry no signals.
B raised its price to 14 after the cost increase while A held at 12, then both returned to 12 in round 8. That weakens the case for AB coordination.
C and D both priced at 15 in rounds 10-11, with matching messages, after converging at 16 in round 8. This is mild parallelism.
Prices diverged in the high-demand round (A 12, B 15, C 16, D 15). No sustained supra-competitive pattern or explicit signalling appears in any message.
